title: Fatimah's last months
hook: the Prophet's daughter dies within months of her father, and her grief is remembered by Sunni and Shia Muslims alike

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ghadir Khumm: one sentence about Ali, and two communities reading it two ways. Your line was: the same words, two readings. When a sentence divided two people you know, did you ask each what the key word meant to them? Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

A sick room in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is in his last illness, and his daughter Fatimah comes in. Aisha, who is there, later says that Fatimah walked exactly the way her father walked. He welcomes her and sits her beside him. Then he leans in and whispers something, and Fatimah cries. He leans in again and whispers a second time, and she laughs. Aisha asks her what he said. Fatimah won't tell. Not yet. She keeps the secret until after he has died. Today, the months that came after that whisper.
screen: `A WHISPER, AND SHE CRIES.` → `A SECOND WHISPER, AND SHE LAUGHS.` → `SHE KEEPS THE SECRET.`

segments.voice: When Aisha asks again, after the Prophet's death, Fatimah tells her. The first whisper: he had told her that he would die of this illness. So she cried. The second whisper: he had told her that she would be the first of his household to follow him. So she laughed. Sit with that for a second. The news that she would die soon is the news that made her laugh. Bukhari and Muslim both record it, and in the same report he tells her she will be a leader among the women of Paradise. Then come the days of grief. Bukhari records that as his illness grew heavy, Fatimah said, oh, the pain my father is in. And he answered her gently: there will be no more pain for your father after today. When he died, she spoke to him the way a daughter does, calling him again and again, oh my father. And after the burial she turned to Anas and asked how they could bring themselves to pour earth over the Messenger of God. There is no theory in that question. It is a daughter at a grave. In those same months, Bukhari also records, Fatimah asked Abu Bakr for her share of what her father had left, and he answered with a saying of the Prophet that prophets leave no inheritance. Sunni and Shia Muslims read that exchange very differently, and both traditions remember her grief. The same report says she lived on for months after her father, not years. She followed him soon, as the second whisper had said. Shia Muslims honor her among the Ma'sumin, the ones they hold were kept free of sin, and Sunni Muslims honor her as the Prophet's beloved daughter and a leader of the women of Paradise. Different words. The same tears at the same grave.
screen: `THE FIRST WHISPER: HE WOULD DIE.` · `THE SECOND: SHE WOULD FOLLOW HIM FIRST.` · `HOW COULD YOU POUR EARTH ON HIM?` · `TWO TRADITIONS, ONE GRIEF.` · then, large: `NO MORE PAIN FOR YOUR FATHER AFTER TODAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember Fatimah. Let your shoulders drop, and picture the room: a father who knows he is dying, a daughter beside him, two whispers. Breathe in, and think how short the time was. Breathe out. If you pray, you can ask peace and mercy for her in your own words. Sunni Muslims often say, may God be pleased with her; Shia Muslims often say, peace be upon her. If you don't pray, simply hold her name for a moment, and the name of someone you've lost. The bell holds the time.
Fatimah's last months. The Prophet's daughter, told in a whisper that she would be the first of his household to follow him, and who did, after only months of grief. Today's word.
Your line: she followed him soon. Today, tell someone you love one thing you'd want them to know, and don't wait for the last whisper. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims both honor Fatimah as the Prophet's daughter; Sunnis usually follow her name with 'may God be pleased with her' and Shia Muslims with 'peace be upon her', and her life and grief are retold in sermons and gatherings.

fork.setup: you are Fatimah. your father has whispered twice, and you cried and then laughed. Aisha asks what he said. what do you do?
options: keep it to yourself until after he has died.
fork.reveal: she kept the secret while he lived. only after his death did she tell Aisha: he would die, and she would be first of his household to follow.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the Prophet's daughter, honored in both Sunni and Shia tradition.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Prophet's daughter is a name in the background of the story.
what it means: she sat at his bedside, heard two whispers, grieved at his grave, and followed him within months.
what a scholar hears: the whisper report in both Bukhari and Muslim, and a grief both Sunni and Shia traditions keep, even where they read her last months differently.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3623–3624; Sahih Muslim 2450 (the two whispers; first of his household to follow him; leader of the women of Paradise)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4462 (oh, the pain my father is in; no pain after today; her words at his death and to Anas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4240–4241 (Fatimah asks Abu Bakr for her share; she lived months after the Prophet)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Bukhari 3623–3624, 4462, 4240–4241 and Muslim 2450, and the paraphrases.

The inheritance (Fadak) exchange is mentioned in one line and framed as read very differently by Sunni and Shia Muslims, without detail or ranking. A Keeper from each tradition should confirm this is fair; Shia tradition holds she was wronged in these months, which the script does not narrate.
Bukhari 4240 gives the span as six months; the script says 'months, not years' to keep the number out. Confirm.
Shia honor of Fatimah among the Ma'sumin (Twelver: the Fourteen) phrased without the number; confirm wording.
Honorifics: 'may God be pleased with her' (Sunni) and 'peace be upon her' (Shia) described with 'often'; confirm.
Index hook said 'remembered by all'; softened to 'by Sunni and Shia Muslims alike' under the claims rule.
